At a glance

New Kensington had 12,170 residents in the 2020 census, down from a peak of 25,146 in 1950, and a median household income of $49,063. It grew from the June 10, 1891, land sale, became a borough in 1892 and a city in 1934. The map data holds 5,990 buildings, 6,222 address points and 565 listed places in the city.

Sources: Census Bureau, newkensingtoncatholic.org, Wikipedia, Britannica

A New Kensington mailing address doesn’t always mean the city. In the map data, 217 places outside the city line give New Kensington as their town: 84 in Lower Burrell, 45 in Upper Burrell, 34 in Plum, 33 in Arnold and 21 in Allegheny Township. The counts on this page follow the city line.

Parks

Memorial Park. Main city park with large/small pavilions (resident rates $35–$50); seasonal Memorial Day–Labor Day; reservations 724-335-5421.

1500 Stevenson Blvd., New Kensington · Map it · Source: ReadyLink

Valley Points Family YMCA. Regional YMCA with pools, group exercise, child care and youth sports; phone 724-335-9191.

800 Constitution Blvd., New Kensington · Map it · Source: vpfymca.org

Safety

New Kensington police reported 54 violent crimes to the FBI in 2024, or 4.6 per 1,000 residents, up from 40 (3.4 per 1,000) in 2023. That is the city's highest rate since 2019 (5.3). Property crime rose to 24.0 per 1,000 from 21.2, still lower than any year from 2001 through 2019. Police cleared 32 of the 54 violent crimes.

19 news-reported incidents in New Kensington are on the police blotter, the earliest from 2020.

Source: FBI UCR via Jacob Kaplan

Serious crashes

PennDOT recorded 70 crashes in New Kensington from 2005 through 2024 that killed or seriously injured someone. They killed 16 people and seriously injured 68.

Neighborhoods and landmarks

Neighborhoods

Parnassus. The oldest part of town. The name dates to a 1769 land tract, and Fort Crawford (1777) stood at the mouth of Pucketa Creek here. It was an independent borough from 1872 until New Kensington absorbed it (1931 per Britannica; some sources say 1939). Trinity/Citizens General Hospital began here in 1912, and residents were rescued by rowboat in the 1936 flood.

Source: Parnassus Pen

Downtown / Fifth Avenue. The 1891 street grid of avenues running parallel to the river and numbered cross streets. It is a National Register historic district of 143 buildings (1891-1947) and now the five-block 'Corridor of Innovation', home to the Digital Foundry, Corner LaunchBox, WCCC, Voodoo Brewing and Fridays on Fifth.

Source: Wikipedia

Valley Heights. A New Kensington neighborhood. The Tarentum Bridge opened in 1952 as the 'Tarentum-Valley Heights Bridge'.

Source: Wikipedia

Mount Vernon. A quiet residential neighborhood in the southeast of New Kensington with about 497 residents. Most homes were built between 1940 and 1969.

Source: neighborhoodscout.com

Valley Camp. Listed as a New Kensington neighborhood.

Source: Parnassus Pen

Pine Manor. Listed as a New Kensington neighborhood, along with Parnassus, Mount Vernon, Valley Camp, Valley Heights and '40 Acres'.

Source: Wikipedia

40 Acres. Listed as a New Kensington neighborhood.

Source: Wikipedia

Landmarks

New Kensington Downtown Historic District. National Register district (1998) of 143 contributing buildings from about 1891-1947. Highlights include the Mellon Bank Building (1900), PNC Bank (1914), the Wear Ever Building (1914-15), the U.S. Post Office (1933), the Ritz (1921-22), the Datola (1942) and Columbus (1927) theaters, and a White Castle restaurant (c. 1921-28).

Central business district, New Kensington · Map it · Source: Wikipedia

New Kensington Production Works Historic District (Alcoa works). A 60-acre National Register district (May 7, 1998) with 35 industrial buildings from about 1899-1947. It includes Alcoa's original plant, which operated from 1891 to 1971, and is documented as HAER PA-337.

Along the Allegheny River, Seventh/Ninth Street to Sixteenth Street (New Kensington-Arnold) · Source: Wikipedia

New Kensington Advanced Manufacturing Park. The former Alcoa works and later Schreiber Industrial Park, straddling the New Kensington-Arnold line. It has been owned by a WCIDC-RIDC joint venture since 2023, and Re:Build Manufacturing operates there.

New Kensington / Arnold riverfront · Source: Westmoreland County

Alcoa Research Laboratory / AK Research Park. Henry Hornbostel's limestone laboratory (1928-30), decorated with aluminum doors and fittings and documented as HAER PA-295. It has been redeveloped as AK Research Park since 2011.

Freeport Road, New Kensington · Source: Library of Congress

Mount St. Peter Church. An Art Deco and International-style Catholic church (1942, architect Enos Cooke). Its ceiling is gold tile modeled on Santa Maria Maggiore, and its altar is modeled on St. Peter's Basilica. The parish hosts the yearly Festa Italiana.

100 Freeport Road, New Kensington · Source: Wikipedia

All 16 landmarks

Memorial Park. A city park of at least 25 acres with veterans' monuments, including the original World War I memorial, an M5 anti-tank gun and an F-80 jet fighter.

Stevenson Boulevard, New Kensington · Map it · Source: legion.org

Willie Thrower statue and historical marker. A statue (2006) at Valley High School's Memorial Stadium and a state historical marker (2003) honoring the NFL's first modern-era Black quarterback.

Valley Junior/Senior High School, New Kensington · Source: Historical Marker Database

Digital Foundry at New Kensington. A 15,044-square-foot smart-manufacturing training and innovation center that opened in 2022. The orange building's sawtooth roof recalls the city's industrial heritage.

855 Fifth Ave., New Kensington · Source: Valley News Dispatch (TribLive)

Ritz Theater / Voodoo at the Ritz. A historic 1920s theater in the downtown historic district, reopened in 2020 as Voodoo Brewing's brewpub.

956 Fifth Ave., New Kensington · Source: Valley News Dispatch (TribLive)

Liberty Theater. A movie theater that opened May 2, 1921. It is documented by HABS/HAER in the Library of Congress.

801 Fifth Ave., New Kensington · Source: Library of Congress

Dattola Theatre (later Kensington Theatre). Opened in 1942 as the New Dattola Theatre, and briefly reopened as the Kensington Theatre showing classic double features.

Downtown New Kensington · Source: cinematreasures.org

Former Citizens General Hospital. A 5.5-acre hospital complex on land Alcoa donated in 1915. The hospital closed in 2000, and the building was vacant in 2026 amid a dispute with its out-of-state owner.

Fourth Avenue and Seventh Street, New Kensington · Source: WPXI

Knead Community Cafe. Western Pennsylvania's first pay-what-you-can community cafe, opened in 2017.

1011 Barnes St., New Kensington · Map it · Source: kneadcommunitycafe.org

Fort Crawford site. Site of a 1777 Revolutionary War stockade at the mouth of Pucketa Creek. Excavations have turned up arrowheads.

Mouth of Pucketa Creek, Parnassus · Source: Tribune-Review archive

George D. Stuart (Tarentum) Bridge. A 1,784-foot continuous-cantilever Pratt deck truss bridge carrying PA 366 across the Allegheny River. It opened in 1952.

PA 366, New Kensington-Tarentum · Source: Wikipedia

C. L. Schmitt (New Kensington) Bridge. A 1927 truss bridge linking New Kensington with East Deer and PA 28.

New Kensington-East Deer · Source: historicbridges.org

History

1769

The name 'Parnassus' appears.

The name 'Parnassus' was used as early as 1769 for a 300-acre tract of land that later became the Parnassus section of New Kensington.

Source: Parnassus Pen

1872

Parnassus becomes a borough.

The borough of Parnassus was incorporated. It stayed independent until New Kensington absorbed it decades later.

Source: Parnassus Pen

1890

'Kensington' planned.

The Burrell Improvement Company picked the level riverfront land south of Lower Burrell for a new city and named it 'Kensington'. The name was later changed to 'New Kensington' to avoid postal confusion with the Philadelphia neighborhood.

Source: Wikipedia

1891

Aluminum works come to New Kensington.

Charles M. Hall's Pittsburgh Reduction Company moved its plant 17 miles up the Allegheny River to New Kensington. It was the company's first major aluminum plant outside Pittsburgh.

Source: Library of Congress

1891

Twelve companies by year's end.

By the end of 1891, New Kensington had 12 companies employing 4,000 people.

Source: rauhjewisharchives.org

1892

Borough incorporated.

New Kensington was incorporated as a borough on November 26, 1892.

Source: Wikipedia

28 more from New Kensington’s history

1901

Wear-Ever cookware founded.

Charles M. Hall and Alfred E. Hunt founded the Aluminum Cooking Utensil Company in New Kensington on October 24, 1901. It sold the Wear-Ever brand, and its top line was called 'Kensington Ware'.

Source: mycompanies.fandom.com

1912

Trinity Hospital chartered.

Trinity Hospital, later Citizens General Hospital, was chartered on December 12, 1912, at 427 Sixth Ave. in Parnassus.

Source: Tribune-Review archive

1913

Alcoa works expand into Arnold.

Alcoa's New Kensington Works expanded across the city line into Arnold.

Source: Wikipedia

1915

Alcoa donates hospital site.

Alcoa donated land at Fourth Avenue and Seventh Street in New Kensington for Citizens General Hospital.

Source: Tribune-Review archive

1927

New Kensington Bridge opens.

The C. L. Schmitt Bridge (New Kensington Bridge) over the Allegheny River opened on June 29, 1927.

Source: structurae.net

1930

Population 16,762.

The census counted 16,762 residents in New Kensington.

Source: Wikipedia

1931

Parnassus absorbed.

New Kensington absorbed the neighboring borough of Parnassus.

Note: Britannica and TribLIVE say 1931; Wikipedia says 1939.

Source: Britannica

1934

New Kensington becomes a city.

New Kensington was incorporated as a third-class city.

Source: Britannica

1936

St. Patrick's Day Flood.

The March 1936 flood hit the whole Pittsburgh region. In Parnassus, residents were rescued from the second floors of their houses in rowboats.

Source: Tribune-Review archive

1940

Population 24,055.

New Kensington's population rose to 24,055 in the 1940 census.

Source: Wikipedia

1950

Population peak: 25,146.

New Kensington reached its peak census population of 25,146.

Source: Wikipedia

1953

Willie Thrower makes NFL history.

New Kensington native Willie Thrower became the first Black quarterback in the NFL's modern era on October 18, 1953, playing for the Chicago Bears.

Source: Wikipedia

1958

Penn State New Kensington founded.

Penn State's New Kensington Center opened in the First Ward School Building downtown. It moved to the former Parnassus Junior High in 1963 and to its Upper Burrell campus in 1966.

Source: newkensington.psu.edu

1965

New Kensington-Arnold School District formed.

The New Kensington-Arnold School District was formed on July 1, 1965. Also by 1965, Alcoa had opened its Alcoa Technical Center in Upper Burrell, having outgrown the Freeport Road lab.

Source: Valley News Dispatch (TribLive)

1966

Wear-Ever headquarters leaves.

The Aluminum Cooking Utensil Company, later Wear-Ever, moved its headquarters from New Kensington, its home since 1901, to Chillicothe, Ohio.

Source: mycompanies.fandom.com

1971

Alcoa New Kensington Works closes.

Alcoa closed its New Kensington Works, which had once employed nearly a quarter of the city. The Schreiber family bought the 66-acre site that year and marketed it as Schreiber Industrial Park.

Source: WESA

1998

Two National Register districts.

The New Kensington Downtown Historic District (143 contributing buildings) and the New Kensington Production Works Historic District (the Alcoa works, listed May 7, 1998) were added to the National Register of Historic Places.

Source: Wikipedia

2000

Citizens General Hospital closes.

Citizens General merged with Allegheny Valley Hospital in Harrison under West Penn Allegheny, and the New Kensington hospital closed. Its building was leased as an outpatient center.

Source: Tribune-Review archive

2009

WCCC New Kensington center opens.

Westmoreland County Community College opened its New Kensington center at 1150 Fifth Ave. in January 2009.

Source: westmoreland.edu

2010

Tom Guzzo becomes mayor.

Tom Guzzo resigned his city council seat to become mayor of New Kensington. He was still mayor in 2026.

Source: Tribune-Review archive

2018

City redevelopment authority buys industrial park.

The Redevelopment Authority of the City of New Kensington bought the former Alcoa works (Schreiber Industrial Park).

Source: Tribune-Review archive

2020

Population 12,170.

The 2020 census counted 12,170 New Kensington residents, 4,772 in Arnold and 11,758 in Lower Burrell.

Source: Wikipedia

2022

Digital Foundry opens.

The Digital Foundry at New Kensington, a 15,044-square-foot smart-manufacturing lab on Fifth Avenue, held its grand opening on June 1, 2022.

Source: psu.edu

2023

Re:Build and the Advanced Manufacturing Park.

In May 2023, Re:Build Manufacturing announced an $81 million project at the New Kensington Advanced Manufacturing Park that it said would create 300 jobs. In October, a WCIDC-RIDC joint venture completed its purchase of the park.

Source: pa.gov

2023

New Kensington Bridge rehab.

The C. L. Schmitt Bridge closed on July 24, 2023, for a $24.59 million preservation project and reopened on September 1, ahead of Labor Day.

Source: unionprogress.com

2025

Re:Build begins production.

Re:Build finished upgrades to a 175,000-square-foot facility in the park, which straddles the New Kensington-Arnold line, and began manufacturing in early 2025.

Source: Valley News Dispatch (TribLive)

2025

Penn State votes to close PSNK.

In May 2025, Penn State trustees voted 25-8 to close seven Commonwealth Campuses, including New Kensington, after the spring 2027 semester. The campuses would admit no new students after fall 2025.

Source: Spotlight PA

2026

Planning the campus's future.

The Economic Growth Connection of Westmoreland ran a public visioning survey, 'PSU (Re)New Kensington Campus', on reusing the Upper Burrell campus. No buyer or decision had been announced.

Source: WPXI
